questions.prompt: The voltage transfer function (voltage gain) of a circuit at frequency \(\omega\) is defined as…
options: \(G_{v}=V_{\mathrm{out}}\times V_{\mathrm{in}}\), a real number in volts squared
\(G_{v}(j\omega)=V_{\mathrm{out}}/V_{\mathrm{in}}\), a complex number (ratio of output and input phasors)
questions.explanation:
A transfer function is the ratio of an output phasor to an input phasor (reader Sec. 2.2). For voltage gain, \(G_{v}=V_{2}/V_{1}=(|V_{2}|/|V_{1}|)e^{j(\phi_{2}-\phi_{1})}\). Its magnitude is the amplitude ratio and its angle is the phase shift.
• The product of voltages is not a ratio and has units of \(V^{2}\).
• The ratio of currents is the CURRENT gain, \(G_{i}\).
• A difference is not a transfer function.

questions.prompt: A transimpedance amplifier (TIA) converts an input current into an output voltage. What are the units of its transfer function \(V_{\mathrm{out}}/I_{\mathrm{in}}\)?
questions.explanation:
Volts divided by amps is ohms, so the transfer function is an impedance-like quantity: a 'trans-impedance' (reader Eq. 2.6).
• Siemens \((A/V)\) is for a trans-ADMITTANCE (output current/input voltage).
• \(V/V\) is a voltage gain; \(A/A\) would be a current gain.
• Watts would be for power, not a ratio of signals.

questions.prompt: A circuit has an input voltage amplitude of 250 mV and produces an output CURRENT amplitude of 5 mA. What is the magnitude of its transadmittance \(K=I_{\mathrm{out}}/V_{\mathrm{in}}\)? (Answer in millisiemens, mS.)
questions.explanation: \(K=I_{2}/V_{1}=5\ \mathrm{mA}/0.25\ \mathrm{V}=0.02\ \mathrm{S}=20\ \mathrm{mS}\). A transadmittance has units of siemens \((A/V)\). Common mistake: dividing 0.25/5 (giving 50, i.e., Ω instead of S).

questions.prompt: A lab measurement of an RC-type low-pass shows that its output lags its input by exactly 45° at \(f=2\ \mathrm{kHz}\). For \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega\tau)\), the phase is \(-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)\). What is the time constant \(\tau\)?
questions.explanation:
\(-\tan^{-1}(\omega\tau)=-45^{\circ}\) ⇒ \(\omega\tau=\tan 45^{\circ}=1\) ⇒ \(\tau=1/\omega\).
\(\omega=2\pi\times 2000=12{,}566\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), so \(\tau=1/12{,}566=79.58\ \mu\mathrm{s}\).
This 'find the corner from the 45° point' is a standard way to identify a first-order system from sinusoidal measurements. Common mistake: \(\tau=1/f=500\ \mu\mathrm{s}\) (forgetting \(2\pi\)).

questions.prompt: For a circuit made only of real-valued R, L and C elements, \(H(j\omega)=1/(1+j\omega\tau)\). What is \(H(-j\omega)\) (the response to the complex exponential \(e^{-j\omega t}\))?
questions.explanation:
\(H(-\omega)\) is found by replacing \(\omega\) with \(-\omega\) everywhere: \(1/(1+j(-\omega)\tau)=1/(1-j\omega\tau)=H(j\omega)*\).
This is not an accident: for a real circuit, \(|H(-\omega)|=|H(\omega)|\) (even) and \(\angle H(-\omega)=-\angle H(\omega)\) (odd) (reader Eqs. 1.49–1.50). It is what makes the output of a real input come out real: \(H(\omega)e^{j\omega t}/2+H(-\omega)e^{-j\omega t}/2\) is a sum of conjugates.
The other choices change the magnitude's sign or keep the phase unchanged.

questions.prompt: An RC low-pass filter with \(\tau=1\ \mathrm{ms}\) is driven by \(v_{s}(t)=10\sin(\omega t)\ \mathrm{V}\) with \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). In sinusoidal steady state, what is the output voltage \(v_{o}\) at exactly \(t=0\)?
questions.explanation:
The filter has \(H=1/(1+j)=0.7071\angle-45^{\circ}\). A sine is just a cosine shifted by 90°, and H applies the same amplitude scaling and phase shift to it:
\(v_{o}(t)=10(0.7071)\ \sin(\omega t-45^{\circ})=7.071\ \sin(\omega t-45^{\circ})\).
At \(t=0\): \(7.071\times\sin(-45^{\circ})=7.071\times(-0.7071)=-5.0\ \mathrm{V}\).
Common mistake: answering 0 V because '\(\sin(0)=0\)'. The input is zero at \(t=0\), but the output is delayed by 45°, so it is not.
questions.figure_alt: Input sine and a smaller output sine that lags it.

questions.prompt: A capacitor's phasor current is I \(=j\omega C\cdot V\). A 1 µF capacitor has voltage \(v(t)=2\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{V}\) with \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\). Using \(j=e^{j90^{\circ}}\), find the current \(i(t)\) at the instant when \(\omega t=60^{\circ}\ (\pi/3\ \mathrm{rad})\).
questions.explanation:
I \(=j\omega C\cdot V=j\cdot(1000)(1\times 10^{-6})(2)=j\cdot 0.002\) A \(=2\ \mathrm{mA}\angle+90^{\circ}\), so \(i(t)=2\cos(\omega t+90^{\circ})\ \mathrm{mA}=-2\ \sin(\omega t)\ \mathrm{mA}\).
At \(\omega t=60^{\circ}\): \(i=2\cos(150^{\circ})=2(-0.866)=-1.732\ \mathrm{mA}\) (equivalently \(-2\ \sin 60^{\circ}\)).
Multiplying by j rotates by +90° (the current leads the voltage). Common mistake: using −90° (+1.73 mA), or forgetting that j is not just 'a factor' but a rotation.

questions.prompt: Preview of transfer functions. A photodiode current \(i_{\mathrm{in}}=0.1\cos(\omega t)\ \mathrm{mA}\) flows into a node where a 1 kΩ resistor R and a 2 µF capacitor C are in parallel to ground; the node voltage obeys \(C\cdot dv/dt+v/R=i_{\mathrm{in}}\). For \(\omega=1000\ \mathrm{rad}/\mathrm{s}\), find the steady-state amplitude of v. (A later skill calls \(V/I\) a transimpedance.)
questions.explanation:
Let \(v=V\ e^{j\omega t}\), \(i_{\mathrm{in}}=\) I \(e^{j\omega t}\): \(d/dt\to j\omega\) gives \((j\omega C+1/R)V=\) I.
\(V/I=1/(1/R+j\omega C)=1/(0.001+j0.002)\ \Omega\), whose magnitude is \(1/\sqrt{0.001^{2}+0.002^{2}}=1/0.002236=447.2\ \Omega\) (phase −63.4°).
\(|V|=0.1\ \mathrm{mA}\times 447.2\ \Omega=44.72\ \mathrm{mV}\).
Common mistake: using R alone (100 mV), ignoring that the capacitor shunts part of the current.

questions.prompt: Preview of noise. A later skill says that white noise with density \(e_{n}\ (V/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}})\) passing through a filter of gain |H| over a bandwidth B has RMS value \(e_{n}\cdot|H|\cdot\sqrt{B}\). An amplifier output has flat noise density \(20\ \mathrm{nV}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}\). A filter with \(|H|=0.5\) from 0 to 1 kHz (and essentially 0 above) follows it. What is the RMS noise at the filter output, in nV?
questions.explanation:
\(v_{n}=e_{n}\cdot|H|\cdot\sqrt{B}=20\ \mathrm{nV}/\sqrt{\mathrm{Hz}}\times 0.5\times\sqrt{1000}\ \mathrm{Hz}=20\times 0.5\times 31.62=316.2\ \mathrm{nV}\ (RMS)\).
This is the 'filtering reduces noise' idea from Fig. 1.24: only the noise inside the passband gets through. Common mistake: forgetting the square root of the bandwidth (giving 10 µV).

questions.prompt: Preview of op-amp frequency response. A closed-loop op-amp amplifier with a low-frequency gain of 10 has the single-pole response \(H(jf)=10/(1+jf/100\ \mathrm{kHz})\). For a 0.1 V amplitude tone at 1 MHz, what is the output amplitude?
questions.explanation:
At \(f=1\ \mathrm{MHz}\), \(f/f_{c}=10\): \(|H|=10/\sqrt{1+100}=10/10.05=0.995\).
Output amplitude \(=0.1\ \mathrm{V}\times 0.995=0.0995\ \mathrm{V}\) (the gain has fallen from 10 to about 1).
Common mistake: using the low-frequency gain of 10 (1 V). This is exactly the frequency-domain limit on how well an amplifier tracks fast signals.
